extracted.intended_audience: researchers and research stakeholders (authors, editors, supervisors, policy makers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on what reporting guidelines are, why they matter, and how to choose and use them to ensure complete, reproducible, and ethically sound research reports across study types (e.g., trials, observational studies, systematic reviews).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a reporting guideline
rubrics_metrics.description: A reporting guideline is “[a] checklist, flow diagram, or structured text to guide authors in reporting a specific type of research, developed using explicit methodology.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat reporting guidelines as structured tools created by consensus; they are prescriptive aids for what to include when reporting a particular study type. Use the EQUATOR Network definition as the canonical understanding when selecting or developing guidelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting guidelines as minimum standards of reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporting guidelines are consensus-based recommendations for minimum standards of reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use guidelines to ensure that papers meet a baseline completeness and consistency. They are intended to be concise, structured, and usable during manuscript preparation to avoid omissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose: improve completeness and quality of papers
rubrics_metrics.description: Using guidelines will lead to more complete papers, increasing the quality of papers at the same time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopting the appropriate guideline during writing helps authors produce manuscripts that are clearer and more informative, which can improve editorial and peer-review outcomes and reader comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intended outcomes of good reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: A reporting guideline aims to ensure readers understand the text, research can be replicated by other researchers, the research can be included in a systematic review, or that it can aid doctors in making clinical decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a manuscript against a guideline, check whether essential information is present to allow critical appraisal, replication, systematic review inclusion, and clinical applicability/translation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical benefits of using reporting guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Using guidelines has ethical advances such as fairly using resources, minimizing risk of harm and maximizing benefit of research; this can lead to a reduction in research waste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider guideline adherence part of research ethics—inadequate reporting can waste resources and potentially cause harm by obscuring limitations or methods. Document adherence to reduce waste and improve ethical practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum content requirement for a reporting guideline
rubrics_metrics.description: A reporting guideline should include at least a clear list of what should appear in a paper and how that list was developed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess guidelines for two core elements: (1) an explicit checklist/element list specifying required report items, and (2) transparent documentation of the development process (consensus methods, stakeholder involvement). Prefer guidelines that provide both.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitted/typical formats of reporting guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporting guidelines take the form of a checklist, flow diagram, or structured text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the format that best fits the study type and workflow: checklists for itemized completeness, flow diagrams for process-oriented studies (e.g., PRISMA flow), and structured texts where narrative structure is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use guidelines during the writing process
rubrics_metrics.description: They are structured and simple tools for researchers to be used during the writing process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate the relevant guideline early—at study write-up and manuscript drafting—to ensure items are addressed rather than retrofitted after peer review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting the appropriate guideline for your study
rubrics_metrics.description: There are hundreds of different reporting guidelines; selecting the right guideline can be made easier using tools such as a flowchart that maps common research methods to guidelines, or a reporting guideline wizard for more specific studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match your study design (e.g., randomized trial, observational study, systematic review) to the corresponding guideline (e.g., CONSORT, STROBE, PRISMA) using decision tools on the EQUATOR website or the provided wizard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target users / stakeholders for reporting guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporting guidelines are important for Researchers, Research Performing Organizations, Policy Makers, Research Supervisors / Mentors, Postdoctoral Researchers, Authors / Editors, Senior Researchers, Doctoral Students, and Professors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When promoting or implementing a guideline, tailor communication and training to these stakeholder groups—each has a role in adoption, enforcement, teaching, or policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtues and values to uphold in reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Key virtues and values listed: Accuracy, Efficiency, Objectivity, Transparency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these values as evaluative lenses when judging manuscripts: check for accurate and precise reporting, efficient presentation of methods/results, objective framing (avoid undue bias), and transparent disclosure of methods and limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Related good practices and misconduct considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Related themes include Publication ethics, Authorship, Reproducability, Responsible research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess reporting not in isolation but alongside ethical practices—ensure authorship is appropriate, reproducibility is facilitated by sufficient methodological detail and data/code availability, and that reporting supports responsible research conduct.
